title: Verbose logging to indicate when optimizer / vacuum / indexing process is triggered, plus number of workers as they are dynamically allocated.
body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

ETL Indexing operation is preventing con-current searching.

In its most basic form, a single indexing operation involves deleting a set of points from a collection, before inserting their replacements. This represents a set of document pages that have changed. Multiple indexing operations can be executed at the same time. Both the point deletion and insertion calls (made via the Python qdrant-client package) DO NOT wait for their task to complete and instead just check for an acknowledged message (i.e. we don't want to hold up the ETL process and qdrant can just work its way through its back log).

However, if an attempt is made to carry out a search on the the same collection targeted by the indexing operation, the search either takes a very long time to complete (> 30s), or it just gives up and times out. If an indexing operation is not being undertaken, the same search returns more or less instantaneously. 

If the point deletion and insertion calls are changed to wait until their respective calls are completed the log output from qdrant seems to suggest that the deletion operation is the one taking a considerable amount of time to complete (30+s). So let's consider the possible issues that might cause this...

- Is the filter used by the point deletion targeting indexed fields from the payload? Yes its targeting the field 'pageId':

Collection details:

			},

			},

}

- Deletion operations are computationally expensive and qdrant gets around this by marking the point deleted rather than actually carrying out the removal. So what could cause the deletion to take so long? Has the optimizer / vacuum process been triggered? Unfortunately there's no log output that indicates that. Has this caused all of the available threads to be eaten up, so incoming requests can't be serviced? How do I know how many workers qdrant has allocated from its worker pool to a specific job (i.e. search / indexing / optimization / vacuum etc)? Given this allocation can be dynamic, it would be very helpful to be able to see this change in the logs. At the moment all we see is the number of available workers at start-up.

- Is the deletion operation triggering an index adjustment? Similar problem to the above, no logging to help diagnose this.

Any suggestions / advice would be really helpful, Thanks - Kev.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
More verbose logging to be able to diagnose issues as described above.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
The only other alternative is to try and build my own image of qdrant, adding debug to achieve the same ends. However my knowledge of its internals and the language its written in is zero, so had I've to commit the time to do this.

> In its most basic form, a single indexing operation involves deleting a set of points from a collection, before inserting their replacements. This represents a set of document pages that have changed. Multiple indexing operations can be executed at the same time. Both the point deletion and insertion calls (made via the Python qdrant-client package) DO NOT wait for their task to complete and instead just check for an acknowledged message (i.e. we don't want to hold up the ETL process and qdrant can just work its way through its back log).
> 
> However, if an attempt is made to carry out a search on the the same collection targeted by the indexing operation, the search either takes a very long time to complete (> 30s), or it just gives up and times out. If an indexing operation is not being undertaken, the same search returns more or less instantaneously.

This should not happen. An ongoing indexing operation should not have a significant effect on search performance. Upsertions should be available immediately for search right after they have been upserted.

Is it possible that your machine is bottle necked, by a slow disk and/or low memory possibly?

> Is the filter used by the point deletion targeting indexed fields from the payload?

Delete by filter can be extremely slow. That may very well be the problem here. Did you configure a payload index by on that field?

Instead, we highly recommend to delete points by their ID directly. You can also just overwrite them with a new value.

> (...) Has the optimizer / vacuum process been triggered? Unfortunately there's no log output that indicates that. Has this caused all of the available threads to be eaten up, so incoming requests can't be serviced? (...)

You can see this in `GET /telemetry?details_level=9&anonymize=false`. It lists a lot of ongoing and past optimizations for each shard you have. It also lists the optimization type.

You could also enable debug or trace logging. If I recall correctly, it will log optimizations then.

> (...) How do I know how many workers qdrant has allocated from its worker pool to a specific job (i.e. search / indexing / optimization / vacuum etc)? (...)

Checking `htop` with thread names enabled might give a good indication. If debug/trace logging is enabled as I described above, it'll log how many cores are allocated for each optimization task.

We don't show this by default because it can be very noisy, being more confusing than helpful.

> Is the deletion operation triggering an index adjustment? Similar problem to the above, no logging to help diagnose this.

That is possible, yes. If you delete enough points, the vacuum optimizer can be triggered.

So again. There is logging, and there are instruments for this. You just have to enable it.

---

Looking at your system info, you have just 2 physical cores. That's probably quite low. I see that you've already manually adjusted the CPU budget for it.

Could you also describe your type of storage a bit more? How many IOPS do you get? What is the latency? I assume it is network attached? You mention that it is a file share, is this something like NFS or mounted block storage?

What does your collection info look like? `GET /collections/collection_name`

Could you set up any reproducable example so we can more easily investigate it?

Hi Tim,

I've had partial success reproducing the issue. Steps:

- Build mock qdrant dataset consisting of 13k points by running either vector_size_768_create_qdrant_data.py [Hugging Face's sentence transformer all-mpnet-base-v2 embedding model], or alternatively vector_size_1536_create_qdrant_data.py [azure openai service text-embedding-ada-002-v2 model]. The former is an opensource alternative for ease of setup vs the latter what we currently use. Both reproduce the problem regardless.

> [!NOTE]
> Each embedding was generated based upon text that had a length of up to 3000 characters. Tried to keep the number of segments as close to the original collection by setting a default segment number of 4. Also kept the max optimization threads to 1 to reflect what the original collection was set to.

- Backup this dataset so repeated experiments can be run on the same dataset to replicate the search / indexing issue.

- Run a testbed which involves performing an index op (delete/insert a single point) X times, whilst also continually performing a search op concurrently. This creates X indexing op's where the point in question already exists and X indexing op's where the point is new. Refer to vector_size_768_test.py and vector_size_1536_test.py respectively, depending on which model was used to create the test data.

This was tested locally using Docker Desktop for Windows and VS Code for running the Python (v3.10) scripts. 

docker image: qdrant/qdrant v1.8.1 (single node)
local resources constrained to: CPU's: 4, Memory: 4 GB
embedding model: all-mpnet-base-v2

Lets frame the problem slightly differently if it helps to understand it easier. All I'm trying to do in the test case is carry out a number of delete/insert operations in one process and concurrently carry out a search in another. The search operation is repeated until the precise number of delete/insert operations that we specify have completed.

The process that does the searching is started first so we can observe its behaviour before and during the concurrently executing delete/insert operations. It is hoped that the search operations will still be able to be carried out, even with a steady flow of incoming delete/insert requests (which you would typically experience during an ETL job), and have a comparable response time.

To facilitate this I created a mock qdrant collection of 13k points, being careful to replicate its configuration as near as I could to the original collection where the problem was first experienced.

What I found was when performing the 1st test run, the search operation that occurs after the continuous run of delete/insert operations has started, does not complete until they have all finished. Under these conditions it took nearly 11 seconds to complete, which equates to the time it took to complete ALL the delete/insert operations.

If the same test is performed for a second time, search operations are responded to alongside delete/insert operations as you would expect in a timely fashion.

In order to re-replicate the 1st runs results, qdrant would need to be re-started.

If I run the same test against the original collection (which was the reason the case was raised in the first instance), no matter how many times I run the tests it exhibits the same behaviour as the 1st test run carried out against the mock data. Hence why I claimed partial success to replicating the original problem. 

Which brings us full circle to the original purpose of the case, to be able to see logging that indicates that certain background operations are being undertaken by qdrant to try and shed some light on why this problem is occurring (i.e. if available processes/threads are being hogged by other operations, which could prevent the search process from being serviced). I've tried setting the log level to both DEBUG and TRACE, and have not seen any evidence of such a background process being fired off, i.e. index optimization, indexing, segment manipulation etc - unless I'm interpreting the logs incorrectly and to be fair I don't know what I'm expected to see (i.e. is it as clear as "Starting indexing optimization"? Or is it abbreviated/termed something else in the logs?). All I need in layman's terms is what I should be looking out for in the logs if something like this is actually happening, or if I'm not seeing it what else could explain it (hence why I also went to the lengths of reproducing the issue with mock data and the test scenario described above - the code of which I included above).

Does that help?

> * It fixes as far as it starts up, however the indexer does not kick into action. Should this not automatically happen with indexing_threshold=1 and max_optimization_threads=1?

No, we don't start indexing automatically on start to prevent crash loops. We actually want to clearly show this with a grey collection status in Qdrant 1.10. To trigger indexing again you can send another update operation.

> If I send a request to change the collections max optimization threads to 1 (when it already equals 1), the index op triggers again and the same exception is raised.

Yes, that's one of the things you can do to trigger it again. It is expected behavior. Here's a documentation draft with a simple example request describing this behavior: https://deploy-preview-779--condescending-goldwasser-91acf0.netlify.app/documentation/concepts/collections/#grey-collection-status

So I've managed to fix the error / issue with our 'live' qdrant collection - by [creating a new collection based upon an existing collection](https://qdrant.tech/documentation/concepts/collections/#create-collection-from-another-collection). The idea here is to adopt the latest default optimization options vs the available hardware - plus by creating a new collection, hopefully get rid of any residual collection errors.

It may be worth noting that if you significantly change your hardware profile (especially CPU's) it could be beneficial to copy your existing collections to new ones in order to achieve the best optimizations / segment arrangement.
